title: 09. Deep Learning: Mixed Precision Training
summary: Mixed precision training uses both FP16 (half precision) and FP32 (single precision) to train models 2x faster with ~50% less memory, while maintaining accuracy. This is now standard practice in modern deep learning.

sections.title: Overview
sections.body:
**Status:** ✅ COMPLETE  
**Last Updated:** December 6, 2025

**Mixed precision training** uses both FP16 (half precision) and FP32 (single precision) to train models **2x faster** with **~50% less memory**, while maintaining accuracy. This is now **standard practice** in modern deep learning.

### What You'll Learn:
- FP16 vs FP32 precision
- Why mixed precision works
- Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)
- Loss scaling for numerical stability
- Memory optimization techniques
- PyTorch AMP implementation
- When to use mixed precision

sections.title: 1. Understanding Floating Point Precision
sections.body:
### Precision Formats:

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

print("\n" + "="*70)
print("FLOATING POINT PRECISION COMPARISON")
print("="*70)

# FP32 (Single Precision) - Standard
fp32_info = {
    'bits': 32,
    'sign': 1,
    'exponent': 8,
    'mantissa': 23,
    'range': '±1.4e-45 to ±3.4e38',
    'precision': '~7 decimal digits',
    'smallest_positive': np.finfo(np.float32).tiny,
    'largest': np.finfo(np.float32).max,
    'epsilon': np.finfo(np.float32).eps
}

# FP16 (Half Precision) - Fast
fp16_info = {
    'bits': 16,
    'sign': 1,
    'exponent': 5,
    'mantissa': 10,
    'range': '±6e-8 to ±65,504',
    'precision': '~3 decimal digits',
    'smallest_positive': np.finfo(np.float16).tiny,
    'largest': np.finfo(np.float16).max,
    'epsilon': np.finfo(np.float16).eps
}

print("\n📊 FP32 (Single Precision):")
for key, value in fp32_info.items():
    print(f"   {key}: {value}")

print("\n📊 FP16 (Half Precision):")
for key, value in fp16_info.items():
    print(f"   {key}: {value}")

print("\n⚖️  Comparison:")
print(f"   Memory: FP16 uses 50% of FP32")
print(f"   Speed: FP16 is ~2x faster on modern GPUs")
print(f"   Range: FP16 max = {fp16_info['largest']:,.0f}")
print(f"          FP32 max = {fp32_info['largest']:.2e}")
print(f"   Precision loss: FP16 has ~3 digits vs FP32's ~7 digits")

# Visualize precision loss
values = [1.0, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, 0.0001, 1e-5, 1e-6, 1e-7, 1e-8]
fp32_values = [np.float32(v) for v in values]
fp16_values = [np.float16(v) for v in values]
errors = [abs(float(fp16) - float(fp32)) / (float(fp32) + 1e-10) 
          for fp16, fp32 in zip(fp16_values, fp32_values)]

plt.figure(figsize=(14, 6))

plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
plt.plot(range(len(values)), [float(v) for v in fp32_values], 
         'b-o', linewidth=2, markersize=8, label='FP32')
plt.plot(range(len(values)), [float(v) for v in fp16_values], 
         'r--s', linewidth=2, markersize=8, label='FP16')
plt.xticks(range(len(values)), [f'{v}' for v in values], rotation=45)
plt.xlabel('Original Value', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Stored Value', fontsize=12)
plt.title('Precision Comparison', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
plt.yscale('log')

plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
plt.bar(range(len(values)), [e * 100 for e in errors], 
        color='orange', edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7)
plt.xticks(range(len(values)), [f'{v}' for v in values], rotation=45)
plt.xlabel('Original Value', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Relative Error (%)', fontsize=12)
plt.title('FP16 Precision Loss', fontsize=14, fontweight='bold')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis='y')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("\n💡 Key Observations:")
print("   • Values > 1e-4: FP16 accurate enough")
print("   • Values < 1e-5: FP16 loses precision")
print("   • Values < 6e-8: FP16 underflows to 0!")
print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 2. Why Mixed Precision Works
sections.body:
### The Magic of Mixed Precision:

```python
print("WHY MIXED PRECISION TRAINING WORKS")

print("\n🎯 Key Insight:")
print("   Not all operations need high precision!")

print("\n📊 Precision Requirements by Operation:")
```

**HIGH PRECISION (FP32) needed:**
✅ Weight updates (small changes accumulate)
✅ Loss computation (numerical stability)
✅ Batch normalization statistics
✅ Master copy of weights

**LOW PRECISION (FP16) sufficient:**
✅ Forward pass (matrix multiplications)
✅ Activation functions
✅ Backward pass (gradient computation)
✅ Temporary activations storage

```python
print("\n💡 Mixed Precision Strategy:")
```

1. Store MASTER weights in FP32
2. Convert to FP16 for forward/backward pass
3. Keep gradients in FP16 (fast computation)
4. Convert gradients back to FP32 for update
5. Update FP32 master weights

```python
print("\n✅ Benefits:")
print("   • 2x faster training (GPU tensor cores)")
print("   • ~50% less memory")
print("   • Same final accuracy")
print("   • Larger batch sizes possible")

print("\n⚠️  Challenges:")
print("   • Gradient underflow (values < 6e-8 → 0)")
print("   • Need loss scaling")
print("   • Some ops unstable in FP16")

print("\n🔧 Solution: Automatic Mixed Precision (AMP)")
print("   • Automatic FP16/FP32 selection")
print("   • Dynamic loss scaling")
print("   • Handles edge cases")
```

sections.title: 3. Loss Scaling - The Critical Technique
sections.body:
### Why Loss Scaling is Necessary:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("LOSS SCALING FOR FP16 GRADIENTS")
print("="*70)

print("\n❓ The Problem:")
print("   • Many gradients are in range [1e-7, 1e-5]")
print("   • FP16 smallest positive value: ~6e-8")
print("   • Small gradients underflow to 0 in FP16!")
print("   • Training stalls or fails")

# Demonstrate gradient distribution
np.random.seed(42)
gradients = np.random.lognormal(mean=-10, sigma=2, size=10000)

# Count underflows
fp32_gradients = gradients.astype(np.float32)
fp16_gradients = gradients.astype(np.float16)
underflows = np.sum(fp16_gradients == 0) - np.sum(fp32_gradients == 0)

print(f"\n📊 Gradient Statistics:")
print(f"   Mean: {gradients.mean():.2e}")
print(f"   Median: {np.median(gradients):.2e}")
print(f"   Min: {gradients.min():.2e}")
print(f"   Gradients that underflow in FP16: {underflows} ({underflows/len(gradients)*100:.1f}%)")

print("\n💡 The Solution: Loss Scaling")
print("""
1. Scale loss by large factor (e.g., 2^16 = 65,536)
2. Backward pass computes scaled gradients
3. Scaled gradients are large enough for FP16
4. Unscale gradients before optimizer step
5. Update works correctly!
""")

# Demonstrate loss scaling
loss_scale = 2**16
scaled_gradients = gradients * loss_scale
fp16_scaled = scaled_gradients.astype(np.float16)
recovered = (fp16_scaled.astype(np.float32) / loss_scale)
underflows_after = np.sum(fp16_scaled == 0)

print(f"\n✅ After Loss Scaling (scale={loss_scale}):")
print(f"   Underflows: {underflows_after} ({underflows_after/len(gradients)*100:.1f}%)")
print(f"   Recovery error: {np.abs(recovered - fp32_gradients).mean():.2e}")

# Visualize
plt.figure(figsize=(15, 5))

plt.subplot(1, 3, 1)
plt.hist(np.log10(gradients + 1e-10), bins=50, alpha=0.7, 
         color='blue', edgecolor='black')
plt.axvline(np.log10(6e-8), color='red', linestyle='--', 
            linewidth=2, label='FP16 underflow')
plt.xlabel('log10(Gradient)', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=12)
plt.title('Original Gradients', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.subplot(1, 3, 2)
plt.hist(np.log10(scaled_gradients + 1e-10), bins=50, alpha=0.7,
         color='green', edgecolor='black')
plt.axvline(np.log10(6e-8), color='red', linestyle='--',
            linewidth=2, label='FP16 underflow')
plt.xlabel('log10(Scaled Gradient)', fontsize=12)
plt.ylabel('Frequency', fontsize=12)
plt.title(f'After Scaling (×{loss_scale})', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.legend()
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

plt.subplot(1, 3, 3)
comparison = np.column_stack([
    [underflows, underflows_after],
])
x = ['Before Scaling', 'After Scaling']
plt.bar(x, [underflows, underflows_after], color=['red', 'green'],
        edgecolor='black', alpha=0.7)
plt.ylabel('Number of Underflows', fontsize=12)
plt.title('Underflow Prevention', fontsize=13, fontweight='bold')
plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3, axis='y')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print("\n⚙️  Typical Loss Scale:")
print("   • Start: 2^16 = 65,536")
print("   • Dynamically adjusted during training")
print("   • Decrease if overflow detected")
print("   • Increase if stable for many steps")
print("="*70)
```

### PyTorch AMP Implementation:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler

print("AUTOMATIC MIXED PRECISION (AMP) - PyTorch")

print("\n📦 Core Components:")
```

1. autocast context manager
- Automatically selects FP16/FP32 for each operation
- Keeps numerically sensitive ops in FP32
- Most matmuls in FP16

2. GradScaler
- Automatic loss scaling
- Dynamic scale adjustment
- Handles overflow detection

### Complete Training Example:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("COMPLETE MIXED PRECISION TRAINING EXAMPLE")
print("="*70)

training_code = """
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.optim as optim
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler

# ============================================================
# SETUP
# ============================================================

# Model
model = YourModel().cuda()

# Optimizer
optimizer = optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weight_decay=0.01)

# Loss
criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

# GradScaler for mixed precision
scaler = GradScaler()

# ============================================================
# TRAINING LOOP
# ============================================================

for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    model.train()
    
    for batch_idx, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(train_loader):
        inputs, targets = inputs.cuda(), targets.cuda()
        
        # Zero gradients
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        
        # Forward pass with autocast
        with autocast():
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
        
        # Backward pass with scaled loss
        scaler.scale(loss).backward()
        
        # Gradient clipping (optional but recommended)
        scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
        
        # Optimizer step
        scaler.step(optimizer)
        
        # Update scaler
        scaler.update()
        
        # Logging
        if batch_idx % 100 == 0:
            print(f"Epoch {epoch}, Batch {batch_idx}, Loss: {loss.item():.4f}")

# ============================================================
# KEY POINTS
# ============================================================
# 1. autocast() for forward pass
# 2. scaler.scale(loss).backward() for backward
# 3. scaler.unscale_() before gradient clipping
# 4. scaler.step() instead of optimizer.step()
# 5. scaler.update() to adjust scale
# ============================================================
"""

print(training_code)
print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 5. Memory Savings
sections.body:
### Calculating Memory Reduction:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("MEMORY SAVINGS WITH MIXED PRECISION")
print("="*70)

def calculate_memory(model_params, batch_size, seq_length=None):
    """Calculate memory usage for FP32 vs FP16."""
    
    # Model weights
    weights_fp32 = model_params * 4  # 4 bytes per param
    weights_fp16 = model_params * 2  # 2 bytes per param
    
    # Activations (simplified)
    if seq_length:
        activations_fp32 = batch_size * seq_length * model_params * 4
        activations_fp16 = batch_size * seq_length * model_params * 2
    else:
        activations_fp32 = batch_size * model_params * 4
        activations_fp16 = batch_size * model_params * 2
    
    # Gradients
    gradients_fp32 = model_params * 4
    gradients_fp16 = model_params * 2
    
    # Optimizer states (Adam: 2 states per parameter)
    optimizer_fp32 = model_params * 4 * 2
    optimizer_fp16 = model_params * 4 * 2  # Still FP32!
    
    # Total
    total_fp32 = weights_fp32 + activations_fp32 + gradients_fp32 + optimizer_fp32
    total_fp16 = weights_fp32 + activations_fp16 + gradients_fp16 + optimizer_fp16
    # Note: Mixed precision keeps master weights in FP32
    
    return {
        'fp32_gb': total_fp32 / (1024**3),
        'fp16_gb': total_fp16 / (1024**3),
        'savings_gb': (total_fp32 - total_fp16) / (1024**3),
        'savings_pct': (1 - total_fp16/total_fp32) * 100
    }

# Example models
models = {
    'ResNet-50': 25e6,
    'BERT-Base': 110e6,
    'GPT-2': 117e6,
    'ViT-Base': 86e6,
    'GPT-3 (175B)': 175e9
}

print("\n📊 Memory Comparison (batch_size=32):")
print("-" * 70)
print(f"{'Model':<20} {'FP32 (GB)':<12} {'Mixed (GB)':<12} {'Savings':<12}")
print("-" * 70)

for name, params in models.items():
    mem = calculate_memory(params, batch_size=32)
    print(f"{name:<20} {mem['fp32_gb']:>10.2f}  {mem['fp16_gb']:>10.2f}  "
          f"{mem['savings_pct']:>9.1f}%")

print("\n💡 Key Insights:")
print("   • Larger models = more savings")
print("   • Activations dominate memory (scales with batch size)")
print("   • Can fit ~2x larger batch in same memory")
print("   • Or train models that wouldn't fit in FP32")

print("\n🎯 Practical Impact:")
print("   • 8GB GPU (FP32): batch_size=16")
print("   • 8GB GPU (Mixed): batch_size=32+")
print("   • Faster training + larger batches = better convergence")
print("="*70)
```

sections.title: 7. When NOT to Use Mixed Precision
sections.body:
### Edge Cases and Limitations:

```python
print("WHEN TO AVOID MIXED PRECISION")

print("\n❌ Don't Use Mixed Precision:")
```

1. CPU Training
- No benefit (CPUs don't have Tensor Cores)
- May actually be slower

2. Older GPUs (pre-Volta)
- No Tensor Core support
- Emulated FP16 is slower than native FP32

3. Very Small Models
- Overhead > speedup
- Example: Model <1M parameters

4. Numerically Unstable Models
- Some custom loss functions
- Certain reinforcement learning algorithms
- When accuracy degrades in FP16

5. Gradient Accumulation + Very Long Sequences
- Accumulated gradients can overflow
- Need careful scale management

6. Some Research Experiments
- When debugging numerical issues
- When reproducibility critical (FP16 can vary)

```python

print("   • Standard CNNs (ResNet, EfficientNet)")
print("   • Transformers (BERT, GPT, ViT)")
print("   • Standard loss functions")

print("   • Typical deep learning tasks")
```

sections.title: 8. Advanced Techniques
sections.body:
### Gradient Accumulation with Mixed Precision:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("GRADIENT ACCUMULATION + MIXED PRECISION")
print("="*70)

gradient_accumulation_code = """
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler

# Setup
scaler = GradScaler()
accumulation_steps = 4

# Training loop
for epoch in range(num_epochs):
    for batch_idx, (inputs, targets) in enumerate(train_loader):
        inputs, targets = inputs.cuda(), targets.cuda()
        
        # Forward pass with autocast
        with autocast():
            outputs = model(inputs)
            loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
            
            # Scale loss for accumulation
            loss = loss / accumulation_steps
        
        # Backward pass
        scaler.scale(loss).backward()
        
        # Accumulate gradients
        if (batch_idx + 1) % accumulation_steps == 0:
            # Gradient clipping
            scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
            torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0)
            
            # Optimizer step
            scaler.step(optimizer)
            scaler.update()
            optimizer.zero_grad()

# Key Points:
# 1. Divide loss by accumulation_steps
# 2. Only step optimizer every N batches
# 3. Don't forget to zero_grad() after update
"""

print(gradient_accumulation_code)

print("\n⚠️  Important:")
print("   • Scale loss by 1/accumulation_steps")
print("   • Careful with batch normalization")
print("   • Monitor gradient scale (may need adjustment)")
print("="*70)
```

### Custom Operation Precision:

```python
print("\n" + "="*70)
print("CUSTOM PRECISION CONTROL")
print("="*70)

custom_precision_code = """
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, custom_fwd, custom_bwd

# Force specific operations to FP32
class MyCustomFunction(torch.autograd.Function):
    @staticmethod
    @custom_fwd(cast_inputs=torch.float32)
    def forward(ctx, input):
        # This operation runs in FP32
        output = some_sensitive_operation(input)
        ctx.save_for_backward(input)
        return output
    
    @staticmethod
    @custom_bwd
    def backward(ctx, grad_output):
        input, = ctx.saved_tensors
        grad_input = some_gradient_operation(grad_output, input)
        return grad_input

# Usage in model
class MyModel(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x):
        x = self.conv1(x)
        x = MyCustomFunction.apply(x)  # FP32
        x = self.conv2(x)  # FP16 (autocast)
        return x

# Alternative: Temporarily disable autocast
with autocast():
    x = model.layer1(x)  # FP16
    
    with autocast(enabled=False):
        x = x.float()  # Convert to FP32
        x = sensitive_operation(x)
        x = x.half()  # Convert back to FP16
    
    x = model.layer2(x)  # FP16
"""

print(custom_precision_code)

print("\n💡 When to Use Custom Precision:")
print("   • Custom loss functions with numerical issues")
print("   • Specialized operations (e.g., NMS, RoI align)")
print("   • Research experiments")
print("   • Debugging precision-related problems")
print("="*70)
```

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
### Mixed Precision Training Overview:

| Aspect | FP32 | Mixed Precision | Improvement |
|--------|------|-----------------|-------------|
| **Speed** | 1x | 1.5-3x | ⚡ 2x typical |
| **Memory** | 1x | ~0.5-0.6x | 📉 ~50% less |
| **Accuracy** | Baseline | Same | ✅ No loss |
| **Batch Size** | Limited | 2x larger | 📦 Better training |
| **GPU Support** | All | Tensor Cores | 🎯 V100+ |

### When to Use Mixed Precision:

✅ **Always Use:**
- Training Transformers (BERT, GPT, ViT)
- Training CNNs (ResNet, EfficientNet)
- Modern GPUs (V100, A100, RTX 30/40 series)
- Production training pipelines

⚠️ **Consider Not Using:**
- CPU training
- Older GPUs (K80, P100)
- Very small models (<1M params)
- Numerically unstable custom losses
- Debugging numerical issues

### PyTorch AMP Template:

```python
from torch.cuda.amp import autocast, GradScaler

# Setup
scaler = GradScaler()

# Training loop
for inputs, targets in train_loader:
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    
    # Mixed precision forward
    with autocast():
        outputs = model(inputs)
        loss = criterion(outputs, targets)
    
    # Scaled backward
    scaler.scale(loss).backward()
    
    # Optional: gradient clipping
    scaler.unscale_(optimizer)
    clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0)
    
    # Update
    scaler.step(optimizer)
    scaler.update()
```
